description: Udec students of bioengineering, aerospace engineering, astronomy, and physics engineering
summary:
SpheriumX is a web tool that turns NASA’s SPHEREx infrared all-sky survey into a practical visualizer for celestial objects beyond our Solar System.

SPHEREx maps the entire sky every six months, observing from opposite sides of Earth’s orbit. SpheriumX cross-matches each SPHEREx source with ESA’s Gaia mission, which provides precise positions, distances and motions for over a billion stars. SPHEREx’s spectra add a second layer of information, helping classify each source by its infrared signature.

We validated the method by entering the coordinates of well-known objects and checking our results against established astronomical databases such as SIMBAD. The result is a tested, reusable method that combines two flagship surveys, one infrared and one astrometric, to explore how the sky changes and to make objects of interest easy to find and understand.
details:
Users enter the right ascension and declination of an object of interest, and the platform displays a field of view centered on that object. The view can be switched between SPHEREx’s six main bands, which span infrared wavelengths from 0.75 to 5 micrometers. The left panel shows the object’s flux in each of the six bands, along with a brief description of the object (including its type, position and velocity) and other relevant information. The bottom panel shows the four different epochs in which SPHEREx has observed the sky during its two years of active mission.

The platform’s main benefit is that it brings together two key missions for observing objects of interest, SPHEREx and Gaia, which observe the sky at different wavelengths: SPHEREx in the infrared and Gaia mainly in the visible spectrum. It gives the general public the chance to study, discover and visualize the sky from their own computer, without having to handle large amounts of data, which makes it far more accessible.

The intended impact is to open up the study of the sky beyond the visible spectrum, giving the public a chance to see and explore the sky through different eyes.

Tools used: Python (mainly the astropy, scipy and numpy libraries), data from the Gaia DR3 and SPHEREx missions, Visual Studio Code and HTML.

The project’s creativity lies in letting users view objects of interest not in just one wavelength but across six different bands and four different epochs. Users can explore both spectral and temporal variation according to their interests, in a simple and friendly way, bringing space observations closer to everyone.

Overall, the design prioritizes user freedom, with a platform built to be as simple and friendly as possible.
